question: What are JSY and JSSK and could we use them for delivery?
answer:
Both are government schemes for delivery, and you may well be able to use them. Please confirm the details with your local ASHA/ANM, since the JSY passage I have is from Odisha.

JSY (Janani Suraksha Yojana) gives cash assistance together with delivery and post-delivery care. It is meant to reduce maternal and newborn deaths by promoting delivery in a health facility among poor pregnant women (INDIA-JSY, p. 3). All pregnant women delivering in government health centres are eligible. In accredited private institutions, only families with a genuine BPL card or SC/ST certificate qualify (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). In Odisha the amounts listed for the mother's package are Rs 1,400 in rural areas and Rs 1,000 in urban areas (INDIA-JSY, p. 4). Registration comes with a JSY card, which you carry to the institution at the time of delivery (INDIA-JSY, p. 21).

JSSK (Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakaram) entitles every pregnant woman to free delivery in public health institutions, including caesarean section, with free transport, diet, diagnostics, medicines, other consumables and blood if required (INDIA-JSSK, p. 2). Free diet is for 3 days after vaginal delivery and 7 days after caesarean (INDIA-JSSK, p. v).

A good next step is to ask your ASHA or ANM about registering and the JSY card.

question: Can you tell whether my scan proves everything is normal if I upload only the first page?
answer: I can't see uploaded documents or scans, so I can't look at your first page, and I can't interpret a scan or say it proves everything is normal. Even with the full report, your doctor is the right person to explain it. The WHO notes that many pregnancy complications, including fetal malformations, may develop later or may not be detectable without appropriate ultrasound training and equipment (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). So one scan cannot prove everything is normal. A single scan before 24 weeks is recommended to estimate gestational age and improve detection of anomalies and multiple pregnancies (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 16). At 18 weeks or later, scans may also look at the baby's head, spine, heart, limbs, and the placenta, where skills and systems allow (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. vii). Scans also don't replace regular antenatal check-ups (WHO-ANC-ULTRASOUND, p. 13). You could ask your doctor: what did the scan assess, what could it not assess, and what follow-up do we need? question: We follow a strict Jain diet. What can the breastfeeding parent eat while meeting nutrition needs?
answer:
Congratulations to you both. Breastfeeding needs extra food: about 600 extra calories and 13.6 g extra protein daily in the first six months (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Here is how a diet can meet this:

- Eat more than usual, 5-6 times a day if big meals are hard (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Mix cereals with pulses, e.g. a paushtik khichari with rice, dal and green leafy vegetables like spinach, plus 1 tsp ghee or oil (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Cereals and pulses combine for good protein (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
- Eat green leafy vegetables daily for iron (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Sprouted or fermented grains and vitamin C fruits like guava or oranges help iron absorption (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).
- Include milk for calcium, beans and dry fruits, and 1-2 seasonal fruits daily (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32; MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177).
- Use iodized salt (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177) and get adequate sunlight for vitamin D (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).

The passages don't cover which foods are Jain-permissible, so please check that with your family or an expert. Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets, which are recommended during lactation (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32).

question: How do we register our babys birth in India if delivery happened in a private hospital?
answer: Congratulations on your baby! For a birth in a private hospital, the law makes the hospital responsible for reporting it: the medical officer in charge, or a person they authorise, must give the birth details to the Registrar (INDIA-CRS, p. 3). Nestling's checklist says the same: the hospital usually reports it, and the certificate comes from the local registrar (INDIA-CRS). A simple plan: 1) Before discharge, ask the hospital staff whether they have reported the birth and how you will receive the certificate. 2) Keep your photo IDs handy. 3) If the baby has no name yet, you can give it to the Registrar later, within the prescribed period (INDIA-CRS, p. 4). Registrars enter births without a fee (INDIA-CRS, p. 2). Please do not delay: a birth not registered within one year needs a magistrate's order and a fee (INDIA-CRS, p. 4). The certificate is a legal document needed later, for example for school admission (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). I don't have a trusted source for the exact time limit or documents your state needs, so please check with the hospital or your local registrar.

question: Is it okay to drink coffee while pregnant?
answer: Good news: you don't have to give up coffee. WHO advises lowering caffeine only if you have a high daily intake, meaning more than 300 mg a day from all sources, including tea, cola, chocolate and energy drinks (WHO-ANC, p. 38). High intake is probably linked with a higher risk of pregnancy loss and low birth weight. Low intake (under 150 mg a day) was not linked with more pregnancy loss (WHO-ANC, p. 39). For a sense of amounts, a cup of instant coffee has about 60 mg, but some café-brewed coffees have over 150 mg per serving. Black or green tea usually has under 50 mg per 250 mL (WHO-ANC, p. 38). Your doctor can tell you what is right for your own health and pregnancy, so do mention how much coffee and tea you usually have at your next visit.

question: My wife is 8 weeks pregnant. What should I do as a first-time father?
answer:
Congratulations! Here are some practical things you can do now, based on the sources I have.

1. Registration and visits: Pregnancy should be registered within 12 weeks, and the first antenatal visit should happen in the first trimester (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7). You could help your wife register and go with her. Keep her Mother and Child Protection card and all her reports together (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).
2. Medicines: No medicine should be taken in the first trimester unless a doctor advises it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7).
3. Plan ahead: The antenatal visits are a chance to make a birth plan and choose the delivery facility (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7). Later, arrange transport, save the ambulance number 108 (or 102 for free transport to a government hospital), and keep an emergency fund (MOHFW-ANC, pp. 28-29). The hospital bag is best packed by about 36 weeks.
4. Emotional and practical support: Pregnancy can be unpredictable, so being ready as a family helps (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7).

For anything about how she is feeling, please ask her doctor.

question: My wife has morning sickness. How can I help without forcing her to eat?
answer: It's lovely that you want to help. Morning sickness in the first trimester may be physiological, and the guidance is gentle, not forceful (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). Things you can do: offer small, frequent meals rather than big ones; keep greasy and spicy food away; and encourage plenty of fluids. If mornings are worst, keep dry foods like roti, paratha, biscuits or toast by the bed for her to eat after waking (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). Green vegetables are also suggested (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). You can also take on household chores so she can rest (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31), and help the family understand her food needs (MOHFW-ANC, p. 30). Please take her to the doctor if the vomiting is excessive, as she may become dehydrated; signs include a dry tongue and passing less urine (MOHFW-ANC, p. 37). Please don't give her any medicine unless a qualified doctor prescribes it (MOHFW-ANC, p. 31).

question: How can I make a hospital emergency plan before my wife goes into labour?
answer:
Well done for planning early at 34 weeks. Here is a simple emergency plan, based on Nestling's checklist and the guidelines:

1. Know where you will go: the nearest 24-hour PHC for emergency care, and the FRU, which has blood transfusion and surgery (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
2. Arrange transport now. Delay in reaching a facility is a major cause of maternal deaths, so keep a vehicle ready and save the ambulance number: 108, or 102 for free transport to a government hospital (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).
3. Decide who will go with you and who will look after home and children (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
4. Keep an emergency fund and find out about schemes like JSY or JSSK (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).
5. Keep the MCP card, all antenatal records and reports, IDs and insurance papers in the bag, packed by about 36 weeks (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).
6. Learn the danger signs from her doctor or ASHA. If any appear, go to the PHC/FRU immediately, day or night, without waiting (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).

Complications can happen in any pregnancy, so being ready matters (MOHFW-ANC, p. 7). Please ask her doctor which hospital suits her.

question: My parents want a home birth but my wife prefers a hospital delivery. How do I handle this?
answer: It's kind of you to want to keep everyone at peace. Your wife's choice matters most, and it matches the guidance. The MOHFW guidelines say all pregnant women should be encouraged to deliver in a health facility, because complications can develop at any time and are not always predictable (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). A facility has staff, equipment, supplies, drugs and a referral system (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). You could share this with your parents gently, so it is not just your opinion against theirs. Practical things you can do: 1) Back your wife's decision and be her companion; a supportive companion can help a woman face fear and pain (MOHFW-ANC, p. 92). 2) Ask her ASHA or ANM to talk with your parents; they are trained to counsel families on this (MOHFW-ANC, p. 27). 3) Plan transport and save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital), as delay in reaching care is a major danger (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). 4) Pack the bag by about 36 weeks. For anything specific to her health, please ask her doctor.

question: My glucose test was flagged high. Can I fix gestational diabetes by avoiding rice completely?
answer: I'm sorry the result worried you; a flagged test is a reason to follow up, not a reason to panic. WHO describes how GDM is diagnosed using specific blood glucose values (WHO-ANC, p. 48), and it says women with GDM or diabetes in pregnancy require referral and increased monitoring (WHO-ANC, p. 48). The passages don't say that cutting out rice completely fixes GDM, so I don't have a trusted source for that. Please ask your doctor. WHO says GDM treatment usually starts with lifestyle changes, meaning nutritional counselling and exercise, and treatment is effective in reducing poor outcomes (WHO-ANC, p. 48). Because the right plan depends on your health and pregnancy, please don't drop foods on your own. Ask your doctor or a dietitian: Is my result confirmed GDM? What should I eat and how often? How will my sugar be monitored? Do I need any treatment? Your doctor or pharmacist should decide on any medicines. Please book a visit soon.

question: Can I take an overnight bus at 36 weeks to go to my parents house for delivery?
answer: I don't have a trusted source for whether an overnight bus at 36 weeks is safe. Please ask your doctor before you decide, and share your travel plan and the distance. What my sources do say may help you plan. Labour before 37 weeks is pre-term, and the baby may need specialised care at an FRU (MOHFW-ANC, p. 81). Delay in reaching a facility is a major cause of maternal deaths, so know the nearest 24-hour PHC and FRU near your parents' home and how to reach them (MOHFW-ANC, pp. 28-29). Arrange transport and save the ambulance number (108; 102 for free transport to a government hospital) (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Go to a facility without waiting if you notice labour signs such as a bloody sticky 'show' or contractions getting stronger and closer (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). Keep your bag packed with your MCP card and all antenatal records, scan and test reports (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28). I can't see your records, so your doctor can look at them and advise you.

question: I feel anxious about labour and everyone says I should just be happy.
answer: I'm sorry you're feeling anxious about labour, and your feelings are valid even when others urge you to just be happy. The passages don't discuss anxiety directly, but they do show what support looks like. Birth attendants are meant to give emotional support as well as physical care (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39). You can choose the position you find comfortable (MOHFW-ANC, p. 39), you can eat and drink as you wish during labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41), and you should be told what is being done and be asked for consent before a vaginal examination (MOHFW-ANC, p. 41). You should not be left alone during early labour (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43). Knowing the stages may help too: for a first baby, the first stage takes about 12 hours and the second about two hours (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43). Try sharing your worries with your partner, and ask your doctor or midwife at your next visit what your birth plan and support will look like. If anxiety feels overwhelming or affects your sleep or eating, please tell your doctor. I don't have a trusted source in these passages for treating anxiety itself.

question: My neighbour gave me herbal kadha for contractions. Should I take it?
answer: It's kind of your neighbour to think of you. Whether to take this kadha is a question for your doctor or pharmacist, not me. I can't say yes or no to any herbal remedy, because the answer depends on your health and your pregnancy, so please check with your doctor before taking anything meant to bring on or ease contractions. The passages I have don't cover this kadha, so I don't have a trusted source for it. WHO notes that women may turn to traditional healers and herbal remedies, and that women are less likely to engage with services if their beliefs and traditions are overlooked by health-care providers (WHO-ANC, p. 78). So you can raise it openly with your doctor. You could ask: what is in it, and is it safe for me and the baby right now? Also, true labour pain becomes regular and predictable, is felt first in the lower back, increases in duration, frequency and intensity, and may come with 'show', while false labour pain stays irregular and often disappears with walking or sleep (MOHFW-ANC, p. 43). If you are unsure whether what you feel is labour, please talk to your doctor.

question: I had a C-section. How should I plan help at home in the first two weeks?
answer:
Congratulations, and well done on your recovery so far. The passages don't give C-section-specific advice, such as lifting limits or wound care, so please ask your surgeon about those. What they do cover is how to plan the first two weeks.

WHO calls the first two weeks a key time to spot problems and settle into home care (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). It suggests asking yourselves a few questions before discharge: how well you feel physically and emotionally, how confident you and your family are in caring for the baby, and whether your home setup lets someone care for you both (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xvi; p. 152). Planning who helps with baby care, home and any other children fits this, and Nestling's checklist also says to decide who looks after home and children (MOHFW-ANC, p. 29).

Also plan for check-ups: a home visit in the first week by a health worker, or an outpatient visit if that suits you better (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. xiv). Further contacts are advised at 48-72 hours, 7-14 days and week six (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 152). Keep transport and the 108 ambulance number handy (MOHFW-ANC, p. 28).

question: My mother-in-law suggests giving honey to my newborn before breastfeeding.
answer: It's lovely that your mother-in-law wants to welcome your baby with something traditional, and it comes from love. The sources I have, though, suggest gently skipping honey or any other food before breastfeeding. WHO says babies should be exclusively breastfed from birth to 6 months (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 148). It also says not to give breastfed newborns any food or fluids other than breast milk unless medically indicated (WHO-POSTNATAL, p. 149). India's guidelines say that pre-lacteal feeds may not be hygienic and can cause intestinal infections and diarrhoea. They also say colostrum, the first milk, is not harmful and is rich in protective antibodies (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Breastfeeding ideally starts within one hour of birth, and the baby should not even be given water for the first six months (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). A kind way to include her: let her be the one to cuddle the baby after a feed, or to look after you with warm meals and rest. If you'd like more support or have worries about feeding, please talk to your doctor, nurse or a breastfeeding counsellor.

question: I feel I have too little milk on day three. Should I switch to formula?
answer: Feeling worried on day three is very common, and you're not doing anything wrong. In the first few days your body makes colostrum, in small amounts (30-90 ml), and this is enough for a normal newborn (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). Almost all mothers can make enough milk if the baby suckles well and feeds often, and mothers who doubt their supply need support from a skilled person (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Switching to formula is a decision to make with your doctor, nurse or lactation counsellor, who can see you and your baby. Giving other milks or bottles early can reduce suckling and so lower your supply (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). Reliable signs of enough milk are good weight gain and passing urine about six times a day if your baby is exclusively breastfed (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 81). Frequent feeds (at least 8 a day), good attachment and night feeds help (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 123). Please ask for breastfeeding help today, and see a doctor if your baby passes little urine or seems unwell.

question: My family wants me to eat only rice and rasam after delivery. Is that enough?
answer: Congratulations on your baby, and thank you for asking. Rice and rasam alone is not enough while you are breastfeeding. You need more food than usual: about 600 extra calories a day in the first six months, plus extra protein (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Eating 5-6 times a day helps if big meals feel hard (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Rice can stay as your base, but mix it with other foods. Try a khichari of rice, dal and green leafy vegetables with a little ghee or oil (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Add green leafy vegetables daily, 1-2 seasonal fruits, and milk, which is a good source of calcium (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177; ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). Vitamin C foods like guava or orange with meals help your body use iron (ICMR-NIN-DG, p. 32). If you eat eggs, fish or meat, they are good additions; otherwise pulses, beans and legumes can take their place (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 177). Your doctor will advise on iron and folic acid tablets. You could gently share this with your family so they can see you need a fuller plate.

question: Can I give water to my two-month-old in Bengaluru summer?
answer: It's lovely that you're thinking about your baby's comfort in the Bengaluru heat. The guidance is reassuring: for the first six months, babies need only breast milk, with no water, even in the peak of summer. Breast milk has enough water to quench your baby's thirst (MOHFW-ANC, p. 32). Another source says the same: a breastfeeding baby does not need extra water in hot weather, as breastmilk contains all the water a baby needs (MOHFW-IYCF, p. 80). So you can simply breastfeed more often, whenever your baby asks. Feeding on demand is encouraged, and the guideline suggests at least 6-8 feeds in the day and 2-3 at night (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). Please see your doctor if your baby is feeding poorly, or if you are finding breastfeeding difficult. A health worker can also help check attachment and positioning (MOHFW-ANC, p. 62). If family elders suggest water, you can gently share that doctors advise breast milk alone for now.
